name: Binary Search
cs2023: AL: Foundational Data Structures and Algorithms
definition: Binary search finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly comparing the target with the middle element of the current search interval and discarding the half that cannot contain it. It maintains low and high bounds, computes mid between them, and stops when the target is found or when the interval becomes empty (low > high), which means the target is absent. Because each step halves the interval, it needs O(log n) comparisons in the worst case.

roles.name: Sorted array
roles.desc: The input, which must be in sorted order and support direct access to any index.

roles.name: Low bound
roles.desc: Index of the first element of the current search interval.

roles.name: High bound
roles.desc: Index of the last element of the current search interval.

roles.name: Middle index
roles.desc: Index halfway between low and high, e.g., mid = low + (high - low) // 2; the element there is the one compared.

roles.name: Comparison
roles.desc: Comparing the element at mid with the target to decide whether the target is found, lies to the left, or lies to the right.

relations.desc: The input must be sorted by the same ordering used in the comparison; on unsorted input, discarding a half can throw away the target and the result can be wrong.
If the target is present in the array, it always lies within the current interval from index low to index high, inclusive.
mid is always chosen inside the current interval, low <= mid <= high, typically mid = low + (high - low) // 2 (which also avoids integer overflow of low + high in fixed-width languages).
If the element at mid is less than the target, set low = mid + 1; if it is greater, set high = mid - 1; if equal, the target is found. Each update excludes mid and every element on one side of it.
Each step at least halves the remaining interval, so at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons are needed for n elements, i.e., O(log n).

The search ends unsuccessfully when low > high (the interval is empty), which proves the target is not present; updates that fail to exclude mid (e.g., low = mid) can leave the interval unchanged and loop forever.

misconceptions.wrong: Binary search works on any list, sorted or not.
misconceptions.correct: Discarding half the interval is valid only because sorted order guarantees the target cannot be on that side. On unsorted data, binary search can report "not found" for a value that is present.

misconceptions.wrong: Binary search checks about half the elements, so it is O(n/2), which is just O(n).
misconceptions.correct: It halves the remaining interval at every step, so it uses O(log n) comparisons: about 20 for a million elements, not 500,000.

misconceptions.wrong: Setting low = mid or high = mid instead of mid + 1 or mid - 1 is a harmless off-by-one difference.
misconceptions.correct: In the standard inclusive-bounds version, low = mid can leave the interval unchanged (for example, when low and high are adjacent), causing an infinite loop. Each update must exclude mid.

misconceptions.wrong: For a single lookup in unsorted data, sorting first and then binary searching is faster than a linear search.
misconceptions.correct: Sorting costs O(n log n), which is more than a single O(n) linear search. Sorting first pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.

breaks_hint: Dictionary-lookup or guess-the-number analogies capture halving but treat sorted order as a given rather than a hard precondition, and people jump to estimated positions rather than the exact middle. They also skip the low/high bookkeeping and the empty-interval stopping rule, which is where real off-by-one and infinite-loop bugs occur.

quiz.q: What must be true of the array for binary search to work correctly?
choices: It must have an even number of elements
It must contain no duplicate values
Its length must be a power of two
quiz.explain: Sorted order is what makes it safe to discard half the interval after one comparison. Length and duplicates do not affect correctness of finding whether a value is present.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case number of comparisons binary search makes on n elements?
quiz.explain: Each comparison halves the interval, so after about log2 n steps the interval is empty or the target is found.

quiz.q: Binary search runs on [3, 8, 15, 21, 30, 42, 57] (indices 0 to 6) looking for 42, using mid = (low + high) // 2. Which elements are compared with the target, in order?
quiz.explain: low = 0, high = 6, mid = 3: 21 < 42, so low = 4. Then mid = (4 + 6) // 2 = 5: the element is 42, found. Only 21 and 42 are compared.

quiz.q: A sorted array has 1,000,000 elements. About how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case?
quiz.explain: 2^20 = 1,048,576, which exceeds one million, so floor(log2 1,000,000) + 1 = 20 halvings are enough.

quiz.q: A student runs a correct binary search implementation on [9, 2, 7, 4, 5] looking for 9, and it reports "not found." What explains this?
choices: The code must have a bug, since binary search works on any array
The array is not sorted, so after comparing with 7 the search discarded the left half, which contained 9
9 is the first element, and binary search can never find the first element
Binary search only works on arrays with an even number of elements
quiz.explain: mid = 2 holds 7; since 7 < 9, the search sets low = 3 and never looks at index 0 again. Binary search assumes sorted input, and this array is not sorted.

generic_lesson:
Suppose a teacher has 1,000 exam papers sorted alphabetically by student name and needs to find Maya's. Checking papers one by one could take 1,000 looks. Instead, she uses binary search. The sorted stack is the array, and Maya's paper is the target.

She keeps track of two positions: low, the first paper that could still be Maya's, and high, the last. At the start, low is paper 1 and high is paper 1,000. She looks at the paper exactly in the middle, mid, and compares names. If it says Maya, she is done. If the middle name comes before Maya alphabetically, Maya must be later, so she moves low to just after mid. If it comes after, she moves high to just before mid. Either way, the middle paper and an entire half are ruled out, and if Maya's paper exists it is always still between low and high.

This only works because the papers are sorted; in a shuffled pile, ruling out half could throw away Maya's paper. Each step halves what remains, so even 1,000 papers take at most 10 looks, and a million would take about 20. That is O(log n). If low ever passes high, no papers remain to check, which proves Maya's paper is not there, and the search stops.
